cells.tense: What has finished in you is being let go, and your own hand decided it was finished.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: As a standing habit — whenever something between you and someone else feels done, hand back what you've been holding and take back what was yours, and keep no tally of it either way.
cells.core:
The endings you're making lately land at the right hour. Nothing has to break. A thing reaches its completion and you let it stand where it is, because you already knew before it was said out loud. That's felt necessity at work: you stop tending what's done, it stops asking for you, and the next thing gets the room.

So make a habit of closing exchanges through both hands. When something between you and another person feels finished — a standing favour, an ongoing arrangement, a tone you keep taking — hand back what you've been holding and take back what was yours, and keep no tally after. Fairness here isn't arithmetic; it's the ease of something given and returned with no ledger in either direction. What you stop carrying frees the hands for what's next.
cells.sheetLine: You end what's done, and it doesn't have to hurt.
cells.verb: ending what must end so something else can begin
cells.place: the threshold where arrival becomes departure

cells.tense: You will keep clearing things out before they have had a chance to be, and call the clearing freedom.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: One ending you've already scheduled — hold off this week and stay near whoever it touches, keeping your own side while theirs lands, without explaining yourself yet.
cells.core:
The endings are arriving faster than what they end. You can see how each one will go stale, and you clear it from that view alone; from where the other people sit, nothing is given long enough to matter. You're so far ahead that it reads as liberation — and the ones close to you have gone quiet, because you're ending their things on their behalf. Fear can wear freedom's coat.

Before the next cut, take the ending you've scheduled and hold it a week untouched. During that week, stay near whoever it belongs to and feel what it carries for them, keeping your own seat while you do — what they load onto it doesn't have to become your instruction. The endings that come after that week will be the ones worth having, and fewer. What you hold onto for a moment doesn't get stuck; it gets seen.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending what hasn't lived yet and dressing it as freedom.

cells.tense: Something in you was finished before today, and you have kept it running as though the end had not been reached.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Notice where your attention drifts when nothing is asking for it, and follow that pull once — no plan, no permission, just go where it already leans.
cells.core:
You've kept the old form standing. What's in you is finished and you can feel it, and you haven't let it be — you run it as a discipline, as though letting go were a failure of care. It takes hours, and it takes the room something alive could use. The ending you haven't made is waiting on you.

Set the old form down and follow the hour where your attention wants to go anyway. That pull is already a direction; you don't have to manufacture one. Move toward it once, with nothing prepared, and see what the movement gives back. The hours you've spent keeping the dead form upright come home to you — same hours, pointed where they can grow. Moving isn't the opposite of loyalty here. It's how loyalty stops costing you.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping something running that already reached its end.

cells.tense: Something has been ending in you quietly, and you would not say it was you who let it go.
cells.act: give the mess a shape it can be carried in
cells.ask: Put the week you actually had on one page, in the order it happened, and write beside each part whether it is still true — nothing to fix, just the account as it stands.
cells.core:
An ending is under way in you and it has no name on it. A habit, a role, a story about what you're for — it has been thinning, and each time it comes up you think you simply chose to be busy. Your own hand stopped renewing it. Nobody else did that, and nothing has to be announced for it to count.

Look at the week you actually had and put it in order: what you did, and what has already stopped being true. One or two things will show up that you've been carrying past their end without having said so. Write the account plainly, beside each part, still true or not. The page shows what the weeks can't. What you've been carrying past its end is visible now, and once it's visible you can set it down.
cells.sheetLine: Something in you is already ending, and your hand is on it.
cells.verb: ending what must end so something else can begin
cells.place: the threshold where arrival becomes departure

attempts.check: One unsupported claim: that the person is keeping finished things somewhere visible in the present — the record gives the capacity, not what they've kept, so the past-anchored cell says what they're still holding rather than what happened. A reader could reasonably say the ending is not theirs to make or the other people involved won't allow it; the ask to plan one step does not need them to agree, only to be told. The ask survives being wrong because writing the next step does not require there to be an ending, and the sentence that serves me more than them is 'you're bracing against a future you can't write yet' on Too Much — it sounds like a gift and may overreach, so I kept the ask on a floor the person could stand on either way.
